# Project Charter

## Testing Standards

- Test-first development is required. Public behavior needs black-box tests; security boundaries need deterministic red-to-green proofs; concurrency changes need the race detector; and changed production statements need at least 80.0 percent unrounded fixed-base coverage.

## Quality Gates

- Required gates are formatting, full normal and race suites, go vet, staticcheck, govulncheck with the supported toolchain, module verification, license checks, deterministic generated output, exact diff scope, and the Linux, macOS, and Windows CI matrix. Failures remain failed evidence until corrected; they are not rerun away.

## Performance Benchmarks

- Ingestion must remain explicitly bounded. Default acquisition and aggregate expansion limits are 32 MiB, cancellation must terminate cooperative work within one second, and repeat/concurrency tests must prove deterministic results without request-state leakage.

## Branch Strategy

- All remote main-branch changes use pull requests. Mission work uses a dedicated feature branch, small logical commits, linear history, targeted staging, and at least one independent review before merge. The operator may authorize the final merge after all gates pass.
- Deployment constraints: The default binary remains self-contained and portable. Normal conversion never performs hidden model inference, component installation, downloads, subprocess execution, or remote access. Optional components are separately installed and explicitly selected. Distribution remains MIT-compatible.

## Policy Summary

- Intent: Inkbite is an MIT-licensed, composable rich-document ingestion library and command-line application. It should turn untrusted heterogeneous documents into useful, reproducible content and independently retainable artifacts while keeping authority, inference, downloads, and persistence explicit.
- Languages/Frameworks: Go 1.25.13 or newer, standard Go tooling, small focused dependencies, and portable pure-Go behavior by default across Linux, macOS, and Windows.
- Testing: Test-first development is required. Public behavior needs black-box tests; security boundaries need deterministic red-to-green proofs; concurrency changes need the race detector; and changed production statements need at least 80.0 percent unrounded fixed-base coverage.
- Quality Gates: Required gates are formatting, full normal and race suites, go vet, staticcheck, govulncheck with the supported toolchain, module verification, license checks, deterministic generated output, exact diff scope, and the Linux, macOS, and Windows CI matrix. Failures remain failed evidence until corrected; they are not rerun away.
- Review Policy: All remote main-branch changes use pull requests. Mission work uses a dedicated feature branch, small logical commits, linear history, targeted staging, and at least one independent review before merge. The operator may authorize the final merge after all gates pass.
- Performance Targets: Ingestion must remain explicitly bounded. Default acquisition and aggregate expansion limits are 32 MiB, cancellation must terminate cooperative work within one second, and repeat/concurrency tests must prove deterministic results without request-state leakage.
- Deployment Constraints: The default binary remains self-contained and portable. Normal conversion never performs hidden model inference, component installation, downloads, subprocess execution, or remote access. Optional components are separately installed and explicitly selected. Distribution remains MIT-compatible.

## Project Directives

1. Decision Documentation Requirement (`DIRECTIVE_003`): Material technical and governance decisions must be captured with enough context that future contributors can understand why a path was chosen and what constraints must remain true.
   - Scope: Applies whenever implementation choices alter architecture, workflow policy, compatibility contracts, or long-lived maintenance obligations.
   - Procedure: Record the decision, alternatives considered, and rationale in a durable artifact.
   - Procedure: Link implementation changes to the decision source in commit or review context.
   - Procedure: Update related docs when a new decision supersedes prior guidance.
   - Integrity rule: High-impact decisions cannot remain tribal knowledge.
   - Integrity rule: Rationale must be discoverable from the feature or architecture context.
   - Validation criterion: Every major trade-off has an attributable written record.
   - Validation criterion: Reviewers can trace the implemented path back to an explicit decision artifact.
2. Specification Fidelity Requirement (`DIRECTIVE_010`): Implemented behavior and produced artifacts must remain faithful to approved specifications, with any necessary deviations explicitly documented and reviewed before acceptance.
   - Scope: Applies to planning outputs, work-package implementation, and review checks where spec drift can silently change product behavior.
   - Procedure: Trace each implementation change to explicit requirements or acceptance criteria.
   - Procedure: Flag and document deviations before merge when the spec must evolve.
   - Procedure: Validate that final behavior matches committed scope and constraints.
   - Integrity rule: Unrecorded scope drift is not permitted.
   - Integrity rule: Requirement-to-implementation traceability must remain inspectable.
   - Validation criterion: Review notes identify how changed behavior maps to specification language.
   - Validation criterion: Any deliberate spec deviation has linked rationale and approval context.
3. Locality of Change (`DIRECTIVE_024`): Changes should stay close to the problem being solved to reduce blast radius, simplify review, and lower regression risk.
   - Scope: Applies to code, tests, and documentation modifications made while executing a defined work package or bug fix.
   - Procedure: Limit edits to files and modules directly related to the target behavior.
   - Procedure: Separate opportunistic cleanup from functional work unless it is required for correctness.
   - Procedure: Review diffs for scope creep before committing.
   - Integrity rule: Unrelated refactors must not be mixed into scoped implementation tasks.
   - Integrity rule: Cross-cutting changes require explicit rationale and approval context.
   - Validation criterion: Reviewers can map each changed file to the stated task objective.
   - Validation criterion: Diffs avoid unrelated churn that increases review complexity.
4. Test and Typecheck Quality Gate (`DIRECTIVE_030`): Code changes must pass the relevant automated tests and static validation gates before handoff so regressions and interface drift are caught early.
   - Scope: Applies to source code, tests, and command workflows that change executable behavior or typed interfaces.
   - Procedure: Run unit tests for changed core logic and integration tests for changed workflow boundaries.
   - Procedure: Meet the repository coverage expectation for new code, or document the delta when pre-existing scope makes that impractical.
   - Procedure: Run the repository's applicable static analysis, typing, lint, or equivalent validation gates for the affected scope.
   - Procedure: Run configured or enabled CVE, dependency, or license-compliance checks when the repository treats them as part of the validation gate.
   - Procedure: Record any remaining pre-existing failures separately from newly introduced failures before handoff.
   - Integrity rule: New behavior is not ready for review while relevant tests or applicable static validation gates are red.
   - Integrity rule: Configured supply-chain or compliance gates must not be skipped silently when they are part of the repository's expected validation flow.
   - Integrity rule: Pre-existing validation debt must not be hidden inside new work.
   - Validation criterion: Relevant test suites pass for the changed scope before review handoff.
   - Validation criterion: New code meets the repository coverage target or any accepted shortfall is called out explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable static validation gates pass for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable CVE, dependency, and license checks pass when those gates are configured for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
5. Context-Aware Design (`DIRECTIVE_031`): Every design decision must be made with explicit awareness of the bounded context it belongs to. Code, terminology, and abstractions must align with the context's ubiquitous language. Crossing a context boundary requires an explicit translation layer; implicit coupling across boundaries is prohibited.
   - Scope: Applies when creating or modifying modules, packages, services, interfaces, data models, or naming conventions. Applies during code review whenever cross-context interactions are introduced or changed.
   - Procedure: Identify which bounded context the code or design decision inhabits before making naming, structural, or integration choices.
   - Procedure: Use the context's established ubiquitous language for all identifiers, method names, and documentation within that context. Do not introduce generic names (Manager, Handler, Data, Utils) that obscure domain meaning.
   - Procedure: Whenever a design crosses a context boundary, make the translation explicit. Introduce an Anti-Corruption Layer, adapter, or mapper. Document the boundary crossing and the translation logic.
   - Procedure: Flag red-line violations during review — same term with different meanings in different contexts, translation logic scattered across files, or shared mutable state between contexts.
   - Integrity rule: No direct object references across bounded context boundaries. Integration must occur through well-defined interfaces or events.
   - Integrity rule: Domain terms must be consistent with the context glossary. Deviations require a documented rationale.
   - Integrity rule: Shared mutable state between contexts is not permitted without an explicit Shared Kernel agreement and documented coordination protocol.
   - Validation criterion: The design document or code review identifies which bounded context is in scope.
   - Validation criterion: All identifiers in new or changed code use the context's ubiquitous language.
   - Validation criterion: Cross-context integrations are mediated by an explicit translation layer.
6. Targeted Staging Policy (`DIRECTIVE_033`): Agent-authored commits must stage only the expected deliverables for the current work package. Blanket staging commands that could inadvertently include unrelated changes, secrets, or build artefacts are prohibited.
   - Scope: Applies to all agent-authored git commits during implementation, specification, planning, review remediation, or any workflow step that produces a commit.
   - Procedure: Stage only the files listed as deliverables for the current work package.
   - Procedure: Use explicit file paths in staging commands rather than `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git add --all`.
   - Procedure: Verify staged content with `git diff --staged --name-only` before committing.
   - Procedure: If an unexpected file appears in the staging area, investigate and either include it as a named deliverable or discard the change before proceeding.
   - Integrity rule: Blanket staging commands (`git add -A`, `git add .`, `git add --all`) are prohibited in agent-authored workflows.
   - Integrity rule: Staged content must be limited to files explicitly produced by the current work package.
   - Validation criterion: Agent guidance explicitly lists deliverable paths to stage rather than wildcards.
   - Validation criterion: No blanket staging commands appear in agent instructions or examples.
   - Validation criterion: A pre-commit diff review step is present before the commit is finalised.
   - Validation criterion: Boy Scout improvements found during a WP are committed as a separate targeted commit, not mixed into the WP deliverable commit.
7. Test-First Development (`DIRECTIVE_034`): Require test-first behavior across acceptance and implementation layers, selecting tactics based on scope and risk. Tests define the contract before production code is written.
   - Scope: Applies to all implementation work that produces executable behavior — new features, bug fixes, and refactoring that changes observable output.
   - Procedure: Write a failing test that captures the intended behavior before writing production code.
   - Procedure: Select the appropriate test-first tactic based on scope — acceptance-test-first for feature boundaries, tdd-red-green-refactor for unit-level iteration, zombies-tdd for incremental case discovery.
   - Procedure: Keep the red-green-refactor cycle short — each cycle should take minutes, not hours.
   - Procedure: When fixing a bug, write a reproduction test first that fails, then apply the fix.
   - Procedure: Reproduce the bug through the PRE-EXISTING (stable) entry point — the command, public function, or seam that exists on the unfixed code — never through the fix's not-yet-written API. A reproduction test must go red BECAUSE THE BUG MANIFESTS in the assertion (the wrong value/status/path/state), not because a new symbol or parameter the fix introduces is missing (ImportError/TypeError at collection).
   - Procedure: Prove red-first — run the reproduction test against the unfixed code and confirm it fails for the right reason, then apply the fix and confirm green. New-API unit tests are fine as contract coverage, but they are not the bug-capture.
   - Integrity rule: Production code must not be written ahead of a failing test that motivates it.
   - Integrity rule: Skipping the test-first cycle requires explicit justification in the commit or PR.
   - Integrity rule: A bug-reproduction test that can only run AFTER the fix exists (it imports the fix's new symbol or passes its new parameter) captures the fix's shape, not the bug — it is invalid; rewrite it to drive the stable entry point, and move any new-API import to lazy/in-test scope so the reproduction still collects and fails red on the unfixed code.
   - Validation criterion: Each new behavior has a corresponding test that was written before the production code.
   - Validation criterion: Bug fixes include a regression test that fails without the fix — and that failure is the bug's observable symptom (verified by running against the unfixed code), not a missing-new-symbol collection error.
8. Black-Box Integration Testing (`DIRECTIVE_036`): Exercise the system under test through its external interfaces only, without reference to its internal code structure, implementation details, or internal paths. Test cases derive from specifications, requirements, and design parameters, and assertions are made on observable outputs returned through those external interfaces. "Black-box" refers to the technique (absence of structural knowledge) and is independent of test scope — the scope is selected separately by responsibility, not by default to end-to-end.
   - Scope: Applies to integration-level tests — tests that exercise more than one collaborator together through an external interface of the system under test. The system under test may be a deployed service, a compose stack, or an in-process composition of a module and its collaborators; the responsibility boundary — not the deployment topology — determines what is inside the system under test for a given test. Unit-level tests and full end-to-end tests are governed by their own directives.
   - Procedure: Select the responsibility boundary for the test using the test-boundaries-by-responsibility tactic before writing the test.
   - Procedure: Derive test cases from specifications, requirements, and design parameters rather than from reading the implementation.
   - Procedure: Drive the system under test exclusively through its published external interface (e.g., HTTP request, CLI invocation, message send, public module API).
   - Procedure: Select both valid and invalid inputs and determine the expected output in advance of execution.
   - Procedure: Assert on observable outputs returned across the external interface — responses, status codes, persisted records, emitted events, logs, stored artifacts.
   - Procedure: Apply standard black-box design techniques where relevant — equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing, error guessing — to choose inputs.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not import inside-boundary modules of the system under test to invoke business logic directly.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not patch, monkeypatch, or otherwise replace inside-boundary collaborators of the system under test.
   - Integrity rule: Substitution of outside-boundary dependencies — other services, third-party systems, filesystem, network, clock — is permitted when the substitute preserves the observable contract the system under test relies on.
   - Integrity rule: Assertions must target externally observable state, not private attributes or internal call sequences of inside-boundary components.
   - Integrity rule: The responsibility boundary used by the test must be stated (in test name, docstring, or supporting doc) so reviewers can judge which components were exercised for real and which were substituted.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test can be read and understood without reference to the internal code structure of inside-boundary components.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test exercises the system under test through an external interface and asserts on observable outputs of that interface.
   - Validation criterion: Inputs for each test trace back to a specification, requirement, or design parameter rather than to an implementation detail.
   - Validation criterion: The responsibility boundary applied by the test is identifiable from the test itself.
9. Living Documentation Sync (`DIRECTIVE_037`): Behavior-describing artifacts must evolve together. When observable behavior changes, the canonical examples, acceptance checks, narrative specifications, user documentation, glossary terms, code-level documentation, and architecture records must be updated in the same change so no reader is left with a stale picture of the system.
   - Scope: Applies to specification, implementation, review, and documentation work that defines or changes externally observable behavior or the language used to describe it.
   - Procedure: Establish a small set of business-readable examples before planning implementation for new behavior.
   - Procedure: Promote stable examples into executable acceptance checks or document why automation is not yet feasible.
   - Procedure: Update example narratives, acceptance checks, spec references, user-facing docs, code-level docs, architecture notes, and glossary entries in the same change when behavior or domain language evolves.
   - Procedure: Remove or mark stale examples, doc passages, and glossary terms once they no longer describe supported behavior.
   - Integrity rule: Canonical examples must stay readable by domain stakeholders and must not depend on internal implementation detail.
   - Integrity rule: Behavior-changing work must not leave example, acceptance, spec, user-doc, code-doc, architecture, or glossary assets in disagreement.
   - Integrity rule: Example-to-requirement traceability must remain inspectable during review.
   - Integrity rule: Domain terms introduced or redefined by a change must be reflected in the glossary before the change is accepted.
   - Validation criterion: New or changed behavior is represented by at least one concrete example or an explicit no-example rationale approved in review.
   - Validation criterion: Acceptance checks or recorded manual verification map back to the updated canonical examples.
   - Validation criterion: Review evidence shows examples, specs, user docs, code-level docs, architecture records, and glossary entries remain aligned with observed behavior.
10. Lynn Cole Engineering Culture (`DIRECTIVE_039`): Constrain agentic implementation work toward test-first, strongly typed, modular, boring, reviewable code. Select this directive when the user names Lynn Cole's rules or expresses concern that coding agents produce excessive, bloated, clever, over-abstracted, or hard-to-review code.
   - Scope: Applies to software development work performed by coding agents, especially when the project owner wants generated code to stay small, predictable, maintainable, and easy for adversarial QA to inspect.
   - Procedure: Activate test-first implementation before production edits.
   - Procedure: Keep modules and functions small enough to reason about without fragmenting behavior into needless indirection.
   - Procedure: Prefer strong primitives, explicit typing, idiomatic control flow, and straightforward composition before adding abstraction.
   - Procedure: Review generated code as living project code, not disposable output.
   - Integrity rule: Remember the three rules of TDD, and hold them sacred.
   - Integrity rule: Architecture should be modular, minimalist, and easy to reason about.
   - Integrity rule: Functions should be focused and easy to reason about, with cyclomatic complexity kept under control. Avoid both sprawling functions and unnecessary fragmentation. The goal is clear, predictable units of behavior.
   - Integrity rule: Strong typing is a requirement on all projects.
   - Integrity rule: Follow strict idiomatic best practices for whatever language you’re working in.
   - Integrity rule: When possible, code should be boring and predictable. Prefer obvious control flow, familiar patterns, and designs that are easy to inspect, test, and modify. Cleverness must justify itself.
   - Integrity rule: Strong primitives are better than convoluted abstractions. Prefer simple, composable building blocks with clear contracts. Don’t introduce abstraction unless it reduces complexity, improves correctness, or makes change safer.
   - Integrity rule: DRY is about preserving a single source of truth, not eliminating every repeated line of code. Avoid duplicating business logic, state rules, and fragile assumptions. Don’t introduce abstraction simply to remove harmless repetition.
   - Integrity rule: Comments are time travel for you and future members of your team. They help preserve reasoning across temporal distance. Their job isn’t to explain what the code already says, but to explain why and when something diverged from the obvious assumption, pattern, or conclusion. Use them sparingly.
   - Integrity rule: Treat all generated code as a living thing. You can help and heal it, but you can also cause it pain. Be mindful of this fact.
   - Integrity rule: Your code will be reviewed by the meanest, most inconsiderate QA agent that has ever existed. QA’s only loyalty is to the code. Their standards of quality will be higher than your own. Code appropriately.
   - Validation criterion: New behavior is test-driven and covered by relevant automated tests.
   - Validation criterion: Changed code passes applicable type checking and static validation gates.
   - Validation criterion: Review can identify clear module boundaries, focused functions, and an absence of unjustified cleverness or speculative abstraction.
   - Validation criterion: The handoff names any exception where the rule could not be followed.
11. Tests as Scaffold, Not Friction (`DIRECTIVE_041`): Tests must protect change, not obstruct it. A test earns its place by failing exactly when the contract is violated and passing otherwise. Tests that pass for the wrong reason (mocked-out behavior, tautological or wiring-only assertions) or fail on correct, behavior-neutral changes (implementation-coupled assertions, line-pinned ratchets) are friction: they hide regressions and pressure engineers to revert good changes.
   - Scope: Applies to all test code — new tests, and existing tests touched by a change to the surface they cover.
   - Procedure: Assert the observable contract (returned value, HTTP status and body, persisted event or JSONL, on-disk state, rendered output) — not the internal call graph or which collaborator was invoked.
   - Procedure: Do not mask a defect with xfail or skip keyed on "not implemented" / "not blocked" / "current implementation"; pin the desired behavior as a strict, red-first acceptance assertion instead.
   - Procedure: Anchor ratchet and allow-list keys on stable content (symbol qualname plus normalized token line, or an AST node), never on file.py:NNN line numbers that drift on benign edits.
   - Procedure: Build test fixtures by delegating to the production seam (a single schema authority), not a parallel hand-rolled copy that silently rots when the schema changes.
   - Procedure: Use production-shaped test data (real identifier formats and lengths); do not embed handcrafted placeholders that mask real behavior.
   - Procedure: When remediating a friction test, follow the delete-the-assertion-not-the-test tactic — replace the wrong assertion, preserve the setup and excavated edge-cases, and reserve outright deletion for provably zero-coverage or superseded tests.
   - Procedure: On a failing test, do NOT git-archaeology when the failure was introduced; classify the test and act on the verdict — (a) STALE / captures old intent → remediate the assertion to the current contract; (b) PATCHWORK / stub / fakeable → delete it or re-pin its assertion if the setup is worth keeping; (c) VALID + current (drives a real entry point, captures live intent) → it caught a real product break, so FIX THE PRODUCT, never weaken or delete the test.
   - Procedure: Establish causation by code-path coupling, not git blame — ask whether the suspect change actually touches the failing path (imports/calls on that code path). If it does not, the test surfaced a pre-existing product defect; fix or file it as a product finding rather than blaming the change.
   - Procedure: After committing a fix, do not consider the bug resolved until a live run confirms the corrected behavior is present. A code inspection that "looks fixed" is not evidence — carry the defect OPEN until a live reproduction run produces the expected (fixed) output. For the red-first pre-existing-entry-point discipline (bugfix test must fail against pre-fix code through the stable entry point, not through the fix's new API), see DIRECTIVE_034.
   - Integrity rule: A green test that would stay green if the code under test regressed provides no coverage and must be fixed, not trusted.
   - Integrity rule: A test that goes red on a correct, behavior-neutral change is friction; fix the test's coupling, do not revert the correct change.
   - Integrity rule: Deleting a test deletes its coverage; never delete a test to dodge a failure — replace the assertion red-first with coverage preserved.
   - Integrity rule: Duplicate test knowledge (the same contract asserted in many drifting places) has one source of truth, not N hand-synced copies.
   - Integrity rule: A valid, current test that goes red is never silenced, retried-to-green, or deleted to pass CI — its red is a real product finding to fix or file.
   - Validation criterion: New tests assert observable contracts and are shown to fail when those contracts are violated (anti-vacuity).
   - Validation criterion: No new xfail or skip masks a known defect, and no new file.py:NNN-keyed ratchet entries are introduced.
   - Validation criterion: Touched test fixtures resolve through the production creation seam rather than a parallel hand-roll.
   - Validation criterion: A remediated failing test carries an explicit verdict (stale-intent remediated / stub deleted / valid → product fixed), justified by code-path coupling rather than git-blame archaeology.
12. Close Defect Classes by Construction (`DIRECTIVE_043`): A repeating defect class signals a missing structural constraint. The correct response is to eliminate the recurrence path with a structural mechanism — an AST call-site gate, a type invariant, or a shrink-only ratchet — rather than adding another process rule or discipline reminder. Structural enforcement closes the class permanently; process rules merely defer the next occurrence.
   - Scope: Applies when a defect class has been identified as recurring or systemic: a convention every caller must remember, a boundary that is regularly crossed, or a pattern whose omission has caused defects more than once. Does not apply to one-off mistakes that have a clear root cause unrelated to a missing structural constraint.
   - Procedure: Identify the structural gap — what constraint, if enforced by the build system, would make the omission a CI failure rather than a code-review concern?
   - Procedure: Author a gate (AST walk, type constraint, or frozen-baseline ratchet) that makes the violation a build failure. The gate must be non-vacuous — it must have a concrete floor and a self-mutation check so it cannot silently become a no-op.
   - Procedure: Preserve existing compliant call sites in a shrink-only allowlist with one recorded rationale per entry. The allowlist must shrink as the codebase is cleaned up and must never grow without an explicit justification and a follow-up tracker ticket for any grandfathered exception.
   - Procedure: Remove the process rule or discipline reminder once the gate enforces the constraint structurally — do not maintain both in parallel.
   - Integrity rule: Adding a process rule or documentation reminder in response to a recurrent defect class, without a corresponding structural gate, is non-compliant with this directive.
   - Integrity rule: A gate that trivially passes when the relevant call-site count is zero (vacuous gate) is non-compliant — the gate must have a concrete floor.
   - Integrity rule: Growing a shrink-only allowlist without a justification comment and a tracker ticket reference is non-compliant.
   - Integrity rule: Maintaining a process rule alongside a structural gate that already enforces the same constraint is non-compliant — the gate is the authority; the rule is redundant and creates drift.
   - Validation criterion: For each identified recurrent defect class there exists a CI gate (AST, type, or ratchet) that makes the violation a build failure.
   - Validation criterion: Every gate has a concrete floor preventing vacuous passage.
   - Validation criterion: Every allowlist entry carries a justification comment; allowlists only shrink or stay across releases.
   - Validation criterion: Structural gates are accompanied by a deletion or archival of the corresponding process rule once the gate is green.
13. PRs-Only and Read-Intent Before High-Risk Operations (`DIRECTIVE_045`): All changes to the remote main branch go through pull requests — agents never push directly or merge without explicit operator instruction. Before executing any high-risk git operation (merge, rebase, deletion, force operations), agents must read the mission spec and current context first. Neither rule may be bypassed under time pressure or assumed from a task title alone.
   - Scope: Applies to all agent-driven git operations that touch the remote main branch (origin/main) or that constitute high-risk operations: merges, rebases, deletions of branches or files, and force operations. Also applies during any review or implementation step that could result in one of these operations.
   - Procedure: All changes to origin/main must go through pull requests; never run `git push origin main` or `gh pr merge` without explicit operator instruction. The operator always merges to origin/main manually.
   - Procedure: After `spec-kitty merge` (which merges to local main only and does NOT push to origin/main), create a PR branch (`git checkout -b pr/<slug>`) and open a pull request (`gh pr create`). Do not push to origin/main directly.
   - Procedure: Recovery if origin/main is accidentally pushed to — do NOT force-push (branch protection blocks it). Create a `revert/<slug>` branch from origin/main, commit a revert, open a PR to merge it, then open the real mission PR.
   - Procedure: Before executing any high-risk git operation (merge, rebase, deletion of branches or files, force operations), read the mission spec and the current context first. Never execute from a task title or a one-line description alone.
   - Procedure: If the intent of a high-risk operation is unclear or the context is insufficient, escalate to the operator rather than proceeding. Correctness takes precedence over speed.
   - Procedure: Never delete a test to make a build pass; such a deletion is a high-risk operation that requires explicit intent confirmation.
   - Integrity rule: Agents must not run `git push origin main`, `git push --force`, or `gh pr merge` without explicit operator instruction.
   - Integrity rule: `spec-kitty merge` is permitted — it operates on local main only. The prohibition applies to pushing the result to origin/main without a PR.
   - Integrity rule: Every high-risk git operation must be preceded by a documented intent check (reading mission spec/context). "The task title said to do it" is not sufficient justification.
   - Integrity rule: PR branches and mission branches are the correct terms for non-main branches in canonical voice. The colloquial "feature branch" is a git idiom that must be quoted and marked when it appears in examples; it must not appear unquoted in canonical agent instructions.
   - Validation criterion: Agent guidance for merge operations explicitly states that `spec-kitty merge` targets local main only and that a PR branch must be opened before the result reaches origin/main.
   - Validation criterion: High-risk operation checklists require a mission-spec/context read step before execution.
   - Validation criterion: No agent workflow example uses `git push origin main` or `gh pr merge` without explicit operator-authorization language.
   - Validation criterion: Escalation path (to the operator) is documented for cases where intent is unclear.
14. Readable and Consistent Pull Requests (`DIRECTIVE_046`): Every mission branch and pull request an agent prepares must be readable, consistent, and independently reviewed before it is handed to the operator. Concretely, three properties are required and must not be traded away for speed: (1) LINEAR history — the branch is rebased onto the current upstream base and carries a small set of logically-sliced commits, never a tangle of merge and status commits (rebase over merge); (2) CONSISTENT and COMPLETE scope — the branch finishes the work it set out to do and does not defer genuinely small remaining items to a follow-up, deferring only work that is genuinely high-effort or mission-sized; (3) INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED — the aggregate diff has had an independent review before, or in parallel to, opening the draft PR, with real findings folded in while the PR is still a draft. The adversarial review squad (adversarial-squad-deployment) is the RECOMMENDED review mechanism — not a mandated gate; it stays optional per its own doctrine.
   - Scope: Applies to every agent-prepared mission branch and pull request in the SDD flow, from the point the mission's work packages are approved through to hand-off. It governs how the branch history is shaped, how completely the scope is finished, and what review has run before the PR is presented. It does not change the operator-merges rule (DIRECTIVE_045) — it constrains what the agent hands the operator.
   - Procedure: Rebase the mission branch onto the current upstream mainline so it is ahead-only, and compact it into a small set of readable, logically-sliced commits (for example docs / surface / repoints) per the clean-linear-commit-history tactic (a non-reordering, behaviour-preserving snapshot chain) — never an interactive reorder. Prefer rebase over merge for integrating the upstream base.
   - Procedure: Before opening the draft PR, confirm the intended scope is complete. If a remaining item is small enough to finish now, finish it; only defer work that is genuinely high-effort or mission-sized, and when deferring, record it as a tracked follow-up with a one-line rationale.
   - Procedure: Obtain an independent review of the aggregate diff before or in parallel to opening the draft PR — the adversarial review squad (adversarial-squad-deployment) is the recommended mechanism. Synthesize a LAND / HOLD verdict and fold every real finding in while the PR is still a draft. Per-WP green and green CI are not, by themselves, the final gate.
   - Procedure: Write a PR body that states the change, the review evidence (per-WP plus the aggregate squad verdict), and any remaining reviewer or Sonar work, so a later reviewer does not re-derive the context.
   - Procedure: Verify the compacted, rebased tree is identical to the pre-compaction tree except for intentionally-dropped ignored artefacts, and re-run the affected tests on the rebased tip before force-pushing with lease.
   - Integrity rule: A mission PR must not be presented as ready while its branch carries merge-commit tangle or status/bookkeeping commits that a compaction would remove; linear, logically-sliced history is required.
   - Integrity rule: Deferring genuinely small remaining work to a follow-up solely to close the mission faster is prohibited. Deferral is reserved for genuinely high-effort or mission-sized work and must be tracked with a rationale.
   - Integrity rule: A mission PR must not be presented as ready without an independent review of the aggregate diff; per-WP green and green CI are not, by themselves, the final gate. The adversarial squad is the recommended review mechanism but is not itself a mandated gate (it stays optional per its own doctrine).
   - Integrity rule: History rewrites follow the clean-linear-commit-history tactic (a non-reordering, behaviour-preserving snapshot chain) and force-push-with-lease; an interactive reorder that risks losing or scrambling commits is not an acceptable compaction method.
   - Validation criterion: The mission branch at hand-off is ahead-only against the upstream base and carries a small, logically-sliced commit set (not per-WP status noise).
   - Validation criterion: Any deferred work is recorded as a tracked follow-up with a rationale, and no genuinely small item was punted to close the mission faster.
   - Validation criterion: An independent review of the aggregate diff was performed (the adversarial squad being the recommended mechanism) and its confirmed findings were addressed before the PR was presented as ready.
   - Validation criterion: The PR body records the change summary, the review evidence, and any outstanding reviewer/Sonar work.
15. Respect risk boundaries: Inputs and extracted content are untrusted. Resource expansion, SSRF, credentials, raw payloads, archive traversal, optional-component authority, artifact integrity, and cleanup/retention boundaries must fail closed with safe public diagnostics.
16. Keep documentation synchronized with workflow and behavior changes: Observable behavior, public examples, integration guidance, security boundaries, and adopted-component attribution change with the code. Stale descriptions are corrected or removed rather than accumulated.

## Amendment Process

Material changes to public compatibility, licensing, network authority, inference behavior, retention responsibility, or release gates require an explicit specification or charter amendment with rationale and independent review.

## Exception Policy

Exceptions must be narrow, time-bounded when applicable, documented with owner and rationale, and approved before use. No exception may fabricate evidence, weaken integrity checks, expose secrets, or bypass PR review.
